newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Pinochet begins farewell to troops.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Pinochet begins farewell to troops.

text.p: Hundreds of soldiers paid homage on Wednesday to former dictator Gen. Augusto Pinochet in the first farewell parade of his final year as Chilean army commander-in-chief.
The colourful march was part of a nationwide tour of military bases by Pinochet, who will step down on March 11, 1998, after more than two decades as army chief.
His imminent retirement has been met with mixed reactions from Chileans who are deeply divided over the legacy of the 81-year-old general who came to power in September 1973 in a bloody coup.

Vilified by leftists as being responsible for thousands of deaths during his military regime, Pinochet is revered by rightists who say he saved the country from ruin by ousting Marxist President Salvador Allende.
"Some Chileans view him with respect, others regard him with fear and awe and some don't like him at all," said Emilio Meneses, politics professor at the Catholic University.

The former general, already one of the world's longest- serving officers, must retire next year under the terms of the 1980 constitution that his own government wrote. He enraged opponents last week by hinting he could stay on in politics by becoming a life senator under the constitution.

"I have thought of becoming a life senator, but it's not something that worries me, as probably when I retire I will spend time with my grandchildren and write about history," the general told El Mercurio newspaper.
Whatever he decides, the constitution gives the armed forces considerable political influence and so Pinochet's shadow will likely loom over Chilean public life after he retires.
Pinochet is expected to be succeeded by his second-in- command, Gen. Guillermo Garin, but the final decision will be made by President Eduardo Frei.
Supporters credit him with introducing free-market reforms that laid the basis for 13 years of uninterrupted growth and made Chile an economic model for the rest of Latin America.
"General Pinochet's work has spread internationally, and he reaches the end of his career in a moment in which his work has been legitimised throughout the world," said rightist deputy Ivan Moreira.

But a government board found that during the 17 years that his military government ruled Chile, nearly 3,200 people died or were classified as "disappeared," meaning that no trace of them was found after they were abducted by security services.
Still, his retirement is unlikely to lead to more trials of military officers for human rights violations.

"The only possibility would be eliminating the 1978 amnesty law, but this is difficult as (even) the government now accepts the law," said Claudio Fuentes of the Latin America Faculty of Social Sciences.
